source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which three features define a true experiment (randomized controlled trial)?
questions.rationale: RCTs have manipulation (intervention), control and random assignment.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 237)
questions.quote: Experiments (or randomized controlled trials [RCTs]) involve an intervention

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Why is the randomized controlled trial considered the gold standard for testing interventions?
questions.rationale: RCTs come closer than any other design to meeting the criteria for inferring causality.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 238)
questions.quote: RCTs are considered the gold standard because they come closer than any other design to meeting the criteria for inferring causal relationships.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which is a criterion for inferring that X causes Y?
options: X and Y must be unrelated
A third variable must explain both
questions.rationale: The cause must precede the effect, there must be a relationship, and it must not be due to a confounder.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 237)
questions.quote: (1) a cause (independent variable) must precede an effect (outcome)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A nurse tests a breastfeeding program in one barangay and compares it with another barangay without the program, with no random assignment. This design is:
questions.rationale: Quasi-experiments have an intervention but lack randomization (or a control group).
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 238)
questions.quote: Quasi-experiments (trials without randomization) involve an intervention but lack a comparison group or randomization.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A study examines whether hours of sleep are related to exam scores among nursing students, without any intervention. This design is:
questions.rationale: Correlational studies examine relationships among variables without intervening.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 238)
questions.quote: correlational studies that examine relationships among variables but involve no intervention.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A study finds that children who drink more soft drinks have more dental caries. The nurse should conclude that:
questions.rationale: Correlation does not prove causation; other factors may explain the association.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 238)
questions.quote: a basic research dictum is that correlation does not prove causation.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Researchers follow a group of smokers and nonsmokers forward for 10 years to see who develops lung disease. This design is:
questions.rationale: Prospective (cohort) designs start with a possible cause and then collect outcome data over time.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 238)
questions.quote: In prospective (cohort) designs, researchers begin with a possible cause and then subsequently collect data about outcomes.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Researchers take children with dengue and children without dengue and look back at their past exposure to stagnant water. This design is:
questions.rationale: Retrospective (case-control) designs start with the outcome and look back for possible causes.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 238)
questions.quote: Retrospective designs (case-control designs) involve collecting data about an outcome in the present and then looking back in time for possible causes.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A survey collects data on the nutritional status of all grade 1 pupils in one week. Data are collected once. This is a:
questions.rationale: Cross-sectional designs collect data at one time; longitudinal designs collect at two or more times.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 238)
questions.quote: Cross-sectional designs involve the collection of data at one time period, whereas longitudinal designs involve data collection at two or more times

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A major problem of longitudinal studies is:
questions.rationale: Longitudinal studies are costly, time-consuming and risk attrition (loss of participants).
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 238)
questions.quote: Longitudinal studies are typically expensive, time-consuming, and subject to the risk of attrition (loss of participants over time)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which method controls all possible confounding variables, even those the researcher has not identified?
questions.rationale: Random assignment balances known and unknown confounders across groups.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 239)
questions.quote: randomization—the most effective method because it controls all possible confounding variables without researchers having to identify them.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: To control for age, a researcher includes only adults aged 30–40 in the study. This technique is:
questions.rationale: Homogeneity restricts participants to reduce variability on a confounder.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 239)
questions.quote: homogeneity (restricting participants to reduce variability on confounding variables)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: During a 6-month study of a weight-loss program, a national anti-obesity TV campaign is launched. This threat to internal validity is:
questions.rationale: History refers to external events during the study that can affect outcomes.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 239)
questions.quote: history (external events that could affect outcomes)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Toddlers' motor skills improved over a 1-year program, but they would have improved with age anyway. This threat is:
questions.rationale: Maturation is change due to the passage of time rather than the intervention.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 239)
questions.quote: maturation (changes due to the passage of time)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Whether study findings hold true for other people, settings and conditions refers to:
questions.rationale: External validity concerns generalizability; internal validity concerns whether the intervention caused the outcome.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 9 Summary (PDF p. 239)
questions.quote: External validity concerns inferences about generalizability

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A researcher surveys whichever patients happen to be in the OPD waiting area that morning. This sampling method is:
questions.rationale: Convenience sampling uses the most readily available people; it is economical but prone to bias.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 266)
questions.quote: Convenience sampling uses the most readily available or convenient people.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A researcher handpicks experienced dialysis nurses because she believes they can best describe the problem. This sampling is:
questions.rationale: In purposive sampling, participants are chosen based on the researcher's knowledge of the population.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 266)
questions.quote: In purposive sampling, participants are handpicked to be included in the sample based on the researcher’s knowledge about the population.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: To ensure equal numbers of male and female students, a researcher sets a target for each and then takes whoever is available in each group. This is:
questions.rationale: Quota sampling fills subgroups by convenience; stratified random sampling selects randomly within strata.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 266)
questions.quote: within each stratum, people are sampled by convenience.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Using the barangay masterlist, a researcher draws names by lottery so every household has an equal chance. This is:
questions.rationale: Simple random sampling selects elements at random from a sampling frame listing all elements.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 266)
questions.quote: Simple random sampling involves the random selection of elements from a sampling frame that enumerates all the elements

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: From a list of 500 patients, a researcher needs 50, so she selects every 10th name. The "10" is the:
questions.rationale: In systematic sampling, population size divided by sample size gives the sampling interval (k).
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 267)
questions.quote: By dividing the population size by the desired sample size, the researcher establishes the sampling interval

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Compared with nonprobability methods, probability sampling is preferred because it:
questions.rationale: Random selection yields more representative samples and allows estimation of sampling error.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 266)
questions.quote: Probability sampling designs, which involve the random selection of elements from the population, yield more representative samples

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which data collection method is used most widely in nursing studies?
questions.rationale: Self-reports (questionnaires and interviews) are the most widely used method.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 267)
questions.quote: Self-reports, which are also called patient-reported outcomes or PROs, involve directly questioning study participants and are the most widely used method

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: An advantage of interviews over mailed questionnaires is:
questions.rationale: Questionnaires are cheaper and allow anonymity; interviews give higher response rates and suit more people (e.g., those who cannot read).
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 267)
questions.quote: interviews yield higher response rates and are suitable for a wider variety of people.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Items rated from "strongly agree" to "strongly disagree" and summed into a total score form a:
questions.rationale: Likert (summated rating) scales score each item and sum them.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 267)
questions.quote: Likert scales (summated rating scales) present respondents with a series of items

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A patient marks her pain on a 100-mm line from "no pain" to "worst pain." This tool is a:
questions.rationale: A VAS measures subjective experiences along a 100-mm line with bipolar ends.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 267)
questions.quote: A visual analog scale (VAS) is used to measure subjective experiences (e.g., pain, fatigue) along a 100-mm line

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: An advantage of biophysiologic measures such as blood glucose readings in research is that they are:
questions.rationale: Biophysiologic measures are objective, accurate and precise.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 268)
questions.quote: Biophysiologic measures have the advantage of being objective, accurate, and precise.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Two nurses independently score the same patients' pressure ulcers and get nearly identical results. This shows good:
questions.rationale: Interrater reliability assesses whether two raters independently assign similar scores.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 268)
questions.quote: interrater reliability (assessing whether two raters or observers independently assign similar scores)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A stress questionnaire given to the same nurses twice, 2 weeks apart, yields similar scores. This tests:
questions.rationale: Test–retest reliability checks the stability of scores over repeated administration.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 268)
questions.quote: test–retest reliability (administering a measure twice in a short period to see if the measure yields consistent scores)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: The degree to which an instrument measures what it is supposed to measure is its:
questions.rationale: Validity concerns measuring the intended construct; reliability concerns consistency.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 268)
questions.quote: Validity is the degree to which an instrument measures what it is supposed to measure.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A panel of experts reviews a new breastfeeding knowledge test to check that its items cover all key areas. This establishes:
questions.rationale: Content validity is whether the instrument's content adequately captures the construct, judged by experts.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 268)
questions.quote: content validity (in composite scales, the extent to which an instrument’s content adequately captures the construct)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Reliability coefficients range from 0.00 to 1.00. Which value shows the best reliability?
questions.rationale: Higher coefficients indicate greater reliability; 0.80 or higher is desirable.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 10 Summary (PDF p. 268)
questions.quote: Reliability is assessed statistically by computing coefficients that range from .00 to 1.00; higher values indicate greater reliability.
